prompt: Why is CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS usually the wrong choice in a migration?
hint: Ask what it checks and what it does not.

choices.text: It checks the name, not the shape
choices.why: A table with a different shape passes silently and your code runs against it.

choices.text: It is refused inside a transaction block
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: It is slower than a plain CREATE TABLE
choices.why: The catalogue lookup is nothing.

choices.text: It refuses to create a table that has an index
choices.why: Indexes are separate objects and irrelevant here.

prompt: CREATE TABLE Invoices works and so does CREATE TABLE "Invoices". What is the difference?
hint: One of them is folded and one is not.

choices.text: They are the same statement written two ways
choices.why: They produce two tables with different names.

choices.text: The quoted one is refused by the parser
choices.why: It is perfectly legal, which is the problem.

choices.text: Two tables; one needs quotes forever
choices.why: Unquoted identifiers are folded to lower case; quoted ones are not.

choices.text: The quoted one creates a temporary table instead
choices.why: Quoting says nothing about lifetime.

prompt: A foreign key is declared on invoices.customer_id. What does that NOT give you?
hint: Two different things are being confused.

choices.text: A refusal when the customer is deleted, under RESTRICT
choices.why: Also what it gives you.

choices.text: A fast way to search by that column
choices.why: A reference is a rule about what may be stored, not a way to search.

choices.text: A record of which table the column points at
choices.why: It is in the catalogue and in \d output.

choices.text: A refusal when the customer does not exist
choices.why: That is exactly what it gives you.

prompt: The convention that lets you tell a date from a moment without looking: a date column ends in ___ and a timestamp column ends in ___.
hint: Two short words, each two letters.

prompt: Where does money go?
hint: One of these stores an approximation of what you wrote.

choices.text: numeric
choices.why: It stores digits, so a thousand additions are exact.

choices.text: bigint, in cents
choices.why: Defensible in some systems, and it moves the scale into every piece of code that reads it.

choices.text: double precision
choices.why: Binary approximation; the total drifts by cents over a thousand rows.

choices.text: real
choices.why: The same approximation with less room.

prompt: SELECT 7 / 2 returns 3. Why?
hint: Look at the types of both operands.

choices.text: SQL performs no decimal division on literals
choices.why: It has, as soon as one operand is decimal.

choices.text: Integer over integer is integer; the rest is dropped
choices.why: Not rounded — discarded. 7 / 2.0 gives 3.5.

choices.text: The column type decides, and there is no column here
choices.why: The literals decide, and both are integers.

choices.text: The result is rounded to the nearest integer
choices.why: Rounding would give 4.

prompt: A table of events inserts and deletes a million rows a day and holds a few million. Which key type?
hint: Ids are not reused when a row is deleted.

choices.text: smallint, because the table stays small
choices.why: It exhausts in under a minute.

choices.text: integer, because the table stays a few million
choices.why: That is the reasoning that produces the outage.

choices.text: uuid, because the range is unbounded
choices.why: It is, and it costs 16 bytes in every index for a problem bigint solves.

choices.text: bigint, because integer runs out in about six years
choices.why: The size of the table is not what exhausts the range; the insert count is.

prompt: Ids in a table read 1, 2, 5, 6. What does that mean?
hint: Where does a number go when a transaction rolls back?

choices.text: Nothing is wrong; rollbacks kept their numbers
choices.why: Any code assuming contiguous ids was wrong the day it was written.

choices.text: The table was loaded from a file with gaps in it
choices.why: Also possible, and not what a gap means.

choices.text: The sequence is corrupt and wants resetting
choices.why: It is behaving as designed.

choices.text: Two rows were deleted and should be restored
choices.why: Possibly, and the gap cannot tell you.

prompt: The clause that makes the database own an id column and refuse one you supply: GENERATED ___ AS IDENTITY.
hint: One word, and its opposite is BY DEFAULT.

prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does varchar(50) buy you over text?
hint: Measure the two and you find one difference.

choices.text: Less disk space per row
choices.why: Identical.

choices.text: A length rule, and nothing else
choices.why: No speed, no space. The storage is identical.

choices.text: An index that fits in memory more often
choices.why: The index holds the same bytes either way.

choices.text: Faster comparisons on short strings
choices.why: They are the same operation on the same representation.

prompt: A UNIQUE email column stores ana@example.com. An insert of Ana@Example.com arrives. What happens?
hint: Equality on text is equality of bytes.

choices.text: It is accepted and silently lowercased
choices.why: Nothing rewrites your value.

choices.text: It is refused as a duplicate
choices.why: Only if the column folds case, which text does not.

choices.text: Accepted — two rows for one person
choices.why: Which is why the fold belongs at write time or in citext.

choices.text: It is refused because of the capitals in it
choices.why: Capitals are ordinary characters.

prompt: Why is char(n) a type to avoid?
hint: Ask what happens to a value shorter than n.

choices.text: It refuses non-ASCII characters
choices.why: It accepts them like any text type.

choices.text: It has a smaller maximum length than varchar
choices.why: The maximum is not the issue.

choices.text: An index on it is refused
choices.why: It can.

choices.text: It pads, so lengths and comparisons disagree
choices.why: 'PT' in a char(5) is 'PT   ' and the spaces follow it around.

prompt: What does timestamptz store?
hint: The name is misleading about one detail.

choices.text: An absolute moment, converted on read
choices.why: It does not store a zone; it stores the instant.

choices.text: The session's timezone at the time of insert
choices.why: The session decides how it is read, not what is stored.

choices.text: A moment and the timezone it was written in
choices.why: The zone is not kept, which surprises people.

choices.text: Digits, like timestamp, with a label attached
choices.why: That would be timestamp with extra text.

prompt: Why is 01:30 on the morning clocks go back a problem for a timestamp column?
hint: Count how many times that reading occurs.

choices.text: It happens twice and the digits cannot say which
choices.why: Two different moments, one value, and sorting them is wrong.

choices.text: That reading does not occur that morning
choices.why: That is the spring transition, not the autumn one.

choices.text: It is stored as UTC and shifts by an hour
choices.why: That is what timestamptz does, and it is the fix.

choices.text: The database refuses to store it
choices.why: It stores it happily, which is the problem.

prompt: Inside one transaction, now() is called three times a second apart. What comes back?
hint: It is named for the transaction, not the clock.

choices.text: Three values a second apart
choices.why: That is clock_timestamp().

choices.text: The session's start time
choices.why: The transaction's, not the session's.

choices.text: An error, since now() is callable once
choices.why: It may be called freely.

choices.text: The same value: the transaction's start
choices.why: Which makes every row of one insert coherent.

prompt: Which belongs in a date column rather than a timestamptz?
hint: Ask whether the thing has a moment at all.

choices.text: A date of birth
choices.why: The same day everywhere; storing it as a moment moves it in another zone.

choices.text: When a parcel was delivered
choices.why: An instant somebody rounded, and the rounding decides which day's report it lands in.

choices.text: When an invoice was paid
choices.why: An instant.

choices.text: When a session expires
choices.why: An instant, and one that must be compared precisely.

prompt: The one rule this section carries, in one word: use ___ rather than timestamp.
hint: One word, and it is a type name.

prompt: is_paid boolean against paid_at timestamptz. Why prefer the second?
hint: Count the questions each can answer.

choices.text: It takes less space on disk per row
choices.why: It takes more.

choices.text: A boolean allows three states
choices.why: Only if you forget NOT NULL, which is a separate fix.

choices.text: Whether and when, in one column
choices.why: And WHERE paid_at IS NOT NULL reads perfectly well.

choices.text: A boolean index is of little use
choices.why: They can, and that is not the argument.

prompt: When has a jsonb column been used to avoid designing a table?
hint: Four symptoms, and they are all about asking questions of it.

choices.text: It holds more than about ten distinct keys
choices.why: Size is not the criterion.

choices.text: It came from another system's API
choices.why: That is the case where jsonb is right.

choices.text: You index a key inside it, or count rows
choices.why: Those are the questions a table answers and a blob does not.

choices.text: Two rows have different keys
choices.why: Expected of a payload, which is what it is for.

prompt: A status list needs a display name in two languages. What does that tell you?
hint: Something wants to be stored next to the value.

choices.text: The column should be jsonb
choices.why: That stores the labels somewhere nothing can join to.

choices.text: A CHECK constraint should list both languages
choices.why: A CHECK tests a value; it cannot carry one.

choices.text: It was data, so it is a table
choices.why: The moment a value needs properties of its own, an ENUM or a CHECK is the wrong home.

choices.text: The ENUM should be given more values
choices.why: More values is not what is being asked for.

prompt: A column has DEFAULT 'draft'. An insert supplies NULL for it explicitly. What is stored?
hint: A default fills a gap, and a value was supplied.

choices.text: An empty string is stored instead
choices.why: Nothing converts NULL to anything.

choices.text: NULL, or a refusal under NOT NULL
choices.why: The default applies only when the column is left out.

choices.text: 'draft', because that is the default
choices.why: Supplying NULL is supplying a value.

choices.text: An error about conflicting values
choices.why: No conflict is detected.

prompt: Why is a generated column the one safe place in this course to store a derived value?
hint: Recall lesson 2's fourth gate.

choices.text: An index on one is refused, so nothing depends
choices.why: They can be indexed.

choices.text: They are recomputed each time a row is read
choices.why: STORED ones are computed on write.

choices.text: Generated columns are faster to read
choices.why: Speed is not what makes a copy safe.

choices.text: The database maintains it, and only it
choices.why: No trigger to write, no code path to remember, no way to drift.

prompt: Why can updated_at not be a generated column?
hint: Look at the rule about the expression.

choices.text: Generated columns may not be timestamps
choices.why: They may be any type.

choices.text: It would conflict with the created_at column
choices.why: The two are independent columns.

choices.text: now() is not deterministic; the expression must be
choices.why: Which leaves a trigger as the only correct mechanism.

choices.text: It would be too slow on a large table
choices.why: Speed is not the obstacle.

prompt: One line separates the two: ___ sets a value once and the row owns it afterwards; GENERATED computes it forever and the row never owns it.
hint: One word, and it is a SQL keyword.

prompt: A table has two CHECK constraints on one column and you did not name them. What is the risk?
hint: Look at the second generated name.

choices.text: Two checks on a single column are refused
choices.why: They are perfectly legal.

choices.text: The second check goes unevaluated
choices.why: Both are evaluated on every write.

choices.text: The trailing number is positional and moves
choices.why: The application's message is attached to a name that moved.

choices.text: The names collide and one is dropped
choices.why: They do not collide; that is what the number is for.

prompt: Why does a named CHECK beat a generated one for the person who hits it?
hint: The name is a message, one layer removed.

choices.text: Named constraints are checked faster
choices.why: The check is identical.

choices.text: A named one is disableable and a generated one is not
choices.why: Neither can be disabled.

choices.text: One name says what is wrong; the other says which
choices.why: It is the error message the user's user eventually sees.

choices.text: Generated names are not stable across PostgreSQL versions
choices.why: A real problem, and it is the migration one rather than this one.

prompt: When does naming constraints stop being optional?
hint: Three cases, and they all become true eventually.

choices.text: When migrations run on several databases
choices.why: A generated name can differ between them, so the migration passes on one and fails on another.

choices.text: When the schema is kept in version control
choices.why: Every schema should be, named or not.

choices.text: When the table has more than ten columns
choices.why: Column count decides nothing.

choices.text: When the table is larger than a million rows
choices.why: Size decides nothing.

prompt: Match each ALTER TABLE to how much work it is.
hint: One touches only the catalogue, one reads every row, one writes every row.

pairs.right: Catalogue only, instant at any size

pairs.left: ALTER COLUMN TYPE integer to bigint
pairs.right: Writes every row, and needs the free disk for it

right_distractors: Runs in the background without a lock
Refused unless the table is empty

prompt: A one-second ALTER TABLE takes the site down. What happened?
hint: It was not the ALTER that was slow.

choices.text: A trigger fired once per row of the table
choices.why: ALTER TABLE fires no row triggers.

choices.text: The rewrite ran out of disk
choices.why: A real failure, and it would fail rather than block.

choices.text: It queued behind a long SELECT, and so did the rest
choices.why: A patient statement blocks every fast one that arrives after it.

choices.text: The lock escalated to the whole database
choices.why: Locks are per table.

prompt: What does SET lock_timeout before an ALTER TABLE buy you?
hint: Think about the outcome you want when the lock is busy.

choices.text: It lets the ALTER run without a lock
choices.why: Nothing removes the lock.

choices.text: It cancels whichever query is holding the lock
choices.why: It cancels yours, not theirs.

choices.text: It makes the ALTER run faster
choices.why: The work is the same.

choices.text: It gives up rather than blocking everything
choices.why: And you try again when the long query has finished.

prompt: DROP TABLE invoices CASCADE. What does CASCADE do?
hint: It is not what ON DELETE CASCADE does.

choices.text: Drops each of the tables in the schema
choices.why: Only what depends on this one.

choices.text: Deletes the rows in tables that reference it
choices.why: That is ON DELETE CASCADE, and a different thing.

choices.text: Refuses if any referencing table has rows
choices.why: CASCADE is what stops it refusing.

choices.text: Drops the constraints, leaves their data
choices.why: The data survives, the rule does not, and nobody is told.

prompt: What does NOT VALID on a new constraint mean?
hint: It splits one statement into two decisions.

choices.text: Apply it from now on; skip what is there
choices.why: New rows are the ones you control; the old ones you fix at your own speed.

choices.text: The constraint is checked but violations are logged
choices.why: Nothing is logged; violations are refused.

choices.text: The constraint lapses at the next restart
choices.why: It is permanent.

choices.text: The constraint is stored and left unenforced
choices.why: It is enforced on every new row.

prompt: Put the four steps of making a column NOT NULL on a live table in order.
hint: The last step is instant only because of what the ones before it proved.
items: Add a CHECK … IS NOT NULL constraint, NOT VALID
Backfill the existing nulls in batches
VALIDATE the constraint, which scans without blocking writes
SET NOT NULL, which is now instant, and drop the helper constraint
trap: The common swap is validating before backfilling — validation of a table that still holds nulls fails, and you are back where you started with a wasted scan.

prompt: Renaming a column is instant and takes almost no lock. Why is it still a three-deploy change?
hint: Two versions of the application run at once during a deploy.

choices.text: The old name stays reserved for a while after
choices.why: Nothing reserves it.

choices.text: Indexes on the column have to be rebuilt
choices.why: They follow the rename.

choices.text: The rename rewrites the table in the background
choices.why: It does not; it is catalogue only.

choices.text: Old code still running selects the old name
choices.why: The statement is fast and the deploy is broken.

prompt: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY failed halfway. What do you have to check?
hint: It leaves something behind, and it is not obvious.

choices.text: Whether the constraint it supported got dropped
choices.why: It supported none.

choices.text: Whether the table was locked and is still locked
choices.why: The lock is released when the statement ends.

choices.text: Whether an invalid index was left behind
choices.why: SELECT indexrelid::regclass FROM pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid.

choices.text: Whether rows were lost during the build
choices.why: An index build never touches rows.

prompt: Which of these cannot be undone?
hint: Two of these are reversible and two are not.

choices.text: DROP COLUMN
choices.why: The data is gone with it.

choices.text: ADD COLUMN
choices.why: Drop it.

choices.text: RENAME COLUMN
choices.why: Rename it back.

choices.text: SET NOT NULL
choices.why: Drop the constraint.

prompt: The pattern for a change no single step can make safely, in two words: ___ and ___.
hint: Add the new thing first; remove the old thing last.
